Blackjack Table Rules That Quietly Change the House Edge

Published September 2, 2026 · 9 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Two blackjack tables can look identical — same felt color, same six-deck shoe, same dealer shuffling procedure — and still hand the house a meaningfully different edge over your money. Our basic strategy guide covers the roughly 0.5% baseline edge you can reach with perfect play under fairly standard rules, and mentions in passing that specific table rules shift that number. This guide is the deeper version: the individual rule variations, the approximate size of each one, and how to read a table's placard in under a minute before you sit down.

In this guide

  1. The blackjack payout: 3:2 versus 6:5
  2. Dealer hits or stands on soft 17
  3. Number of decks in the shoe
  4. Doubling down restrictions
  5. Surrender rules
  6. Splitting and resplitting rules
  7. Reading a table's rules in under a minute

The blackjack payout: 3:2 versus 6:5

This is the single biggest lever on the list, and it isn't subtle once you know to look for it. A natural blackjack (an ace plus a ten-value card) traditionally pays 3:2 — bet $10, win $15. Over the last two decades, a growing number of tables, especially single- and double-deck games aimed at high-volume floors, have shifted that payout to 6:5 — the same $10 bet now wins only $12. That change alone adds well over a full percentage point to the house edge, commonly cited at roughly 1.4 percentage points worse for the player, which dwarfs every other adjustment in this guide combined. It's usually printed right on the felt, so it takes only a glance to check before you sit down.

Dealer hits or stands on soft 17

A "soft 17" is any hand totaling 17 that includes an ace counted as 11 (ace-6, for example). Under S17 rules, the dealer must stand on that hand; under H17 rules, the dealer draws another card, hoping to improve. Because the dealer gets an extra chance to make a stronger hand, H17 tables are worse for players — commonly cited as adding somewhere in the neighborhood of two-tenths of a percentage point to the house edge compared to an otherwise identical S17 table. It's a smaller move than the payout difference above, but it's one of the more common rule differences you'll actually encounter, since many mid-to-high-limit tables still run H17.

Quick tell: most tables print "Dealer must stand on all 17s" or "Dealer must hit soft 17" directly on the layout, usually near the payout line. If it isn't printed, it's worth asking before you buy in.

Number of decks in the shoe

Fewer decks favor the player slightly, all else held equal, mainly because it becomes marginally more likely that the remaining cards are rich in tens and aces after a run of low cards, and because doubling and splitting math work out a hair better with less dilution from extra decks. The gap between a single-deck game and an eight-deck shoe, under otherwise matched rules, is commonly cited at somewhere around half a percentage point. That's real, but it's also often overstated relative to the payout and soft-17 rules above — a 6:5 single-deck table is still a considerably worse bet than a 3:2, S17, six-deck table, even though the deck count alone would favor the single-deck game.

Deck countApproximate house edge under otherwise standard rules*
Single deck~0.15%-0.20%
Double deck~0.40%-0.50%
Four decks~0.55%-0.65%
Six decks~0.60%-0.70%
Eight decks~0.65%-0.70%

*Figures are commonly cited industry approximations assuming 3:2 payout, S17, double after split allowed, and perfect basic strategy adjusted to the specific deck count. Actual numbers shift slightly depending on the exact combination of other rules at a given table.

Doubling down restrictions

Two separate doubling rules matter here. First, whether you can double down on any first two cards or only on specific totals (commonly 9, 10, or 11) — the more restrictive version costs players a small but real chunk of edge, since some of basic strategy's most profitable plays involve doubling on hands like soft 13-18 or a hard 9 against a weak dealer card. Second, whether doubling after splitting a pair (DAS) is allowed — tables that permit it give players more flexibility to press an advantage after a good split, and disallowing it commonly adds roughly one- to two-tenths of a percentage point to the house edge compared to an identical table that allows it.

Surrender rules

Late surrender lets you give up half your original bet, face-down, before playing out a hand you're likely to lose anyway — most commonly used against a dealer's ace or ten when you're holding a hard 15 or 16. It's a small edge, commonly cited at roughly a tenth of a percentage point in the player's favor when available and used correctly, since it turns a handful of the worst possible hands from "likely full loss" into "guaranteed half loss." Early surrender, which lets you surrender before the dealer checks for blackjack, is considerably more valuable but is rarely offered anymore at land-based or regulated online tables. Many tables don't offer surrender at all, so its absence isn't unusual — but its presence is a small, genuine plus for a disciplined player who uses it in the right spots rather than out of general caution.

Splitting and resplitting rules

Most tables allow splitting a pair into two hands and re-splitting up to three or four hands total if you draw another matching card, though some limit you to a single split with no resplitting. Resplitting aces is treated separately and more restrictively almost everywhere — most tables allow only one card on each split ace and don't allow resplitting them at all, which trims a small amount of value compared to a table that treats split aces like any other pair. None of these differences move the needle nearly as much as the payout or soft-17 rules, but they compound with everything else on this list.

Every figure in this guide describes a mathematical shift in the long-run house edge, not a promise about what happens in any single session. Basic strategy under the best available table rules still doesn't guarantee a winning night — it only improves your odds over a large number of hands. See our responsible gambling resources if it ever stops feeling like entertainment.

Reading a table's rules in under a minute

Before you buy in, most of what you need is printed directly on the felt or posted on a small placard near the shoe: the payout ratio (3:2 or 6:5), the soft-17 rule, and often the doubling and surrender rules as well. If any of those aren't clearly posted, it's reasonable to ask the dealer directly — "does the dealer hit soft 17?" and "is surrender offered?" are normal, expected questions at any table. Online and app-based blackjack tables typically list their full rule set in a help or information screen accessible before you place a bet, which is worth checking once per game the first time you play it, since the rules for a given game are usually fixed rather than changing table to table.

Put together, the order of importance is fairly consistent: check the payout first (3:2, not 6:5), then the soft-17 rule, then deck count and doubling/surrender rules as smaller refinements on top. A 6:5 table with every other rule in your favor is still a worse bet than a plain 3:2, H17, eight-deck table with no surrender — the payout rule alone outweighs everything else in this guide.

Frequently asked questions

Which single rule matters most for the house edge?

The blackjack payout ratio. A 6:5 payout instead of the traditional 3:2 adds roughly 1.4 percentage points to the house edge on its own — far more than any other rule variation covered in this guide.

Is a single-deck 6:5 table better than a six-deck 3:2 table?

No, generally not. The deck-count advantage of single-deck play is small compared to the size of the payout penalty from 6:5, so a six-deck table with a full 3:2 payout is usually the better mathematical bet.

Does it matter if I don't use surrender even when it's offered?

Surrender only helps if you use it correctly in the specific situations where basic strategy calls for it — mainly certain hard 15 and 16 totals against a strong dealer card. Skipping it isn't a mistake, but it does mean you're leaving a small amount of available edge on the table.

Do online blackjack games use the same rule variations as physical casinos?

Yes — online and app-based blackjack games are built around the same set of rule variables (payout, soft-17, deck count, doubling and surrender rules), and reputable platforms disclose them in an in-game help or rules screen.
